Malefactor
MAL-ee-fak-ter
noun
From the Latin malefactor, “an evil-doer,” from male (“evilly, ill”) and facere (“to do”); hence one who does evil, a criminal, a doer of wickedness worthy of punishment.

Biblical Definition

A malefactor is an evil-doer — one who does ill, a criminal condemned for his crimes. The word belongs almost wholly to the passion of our Lord, where it is heavy with a terrible irony. Two malefactors were led out with Jesus to be put to death (Luk 23:32), and at Calvary “they crucified him, and the malefactors, one on the right hand, and the other on the left” (Luk 23:33). The sinless Son of God was numbered with transgressors, hung between two criminals as though He were the chief of them — He who did no evil, crucified in the place of evil-doers, that He might bear their evil in His own body on the tree. One of the malefactors railed on Him (Luk 23:39), but the other, rebuking his fellow and owning his own just condemnation, turned to Christ with the dying prayer, “Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom” — and heard the word of paradise. Here is sovereign grace at its plainest: a malefactor, nailed fast in his last hour, with no work to offer and no time to mend, saved by a look to Christ. The word’s bitterest use is on the lips of Christ’s accusers, who told Pilate, “If he were not a malefactor, we would not have delivered him up unto thee” (Joh 18:30) — the world calling the one sinless Man a malefactor, condemning Righteousness itself. So the guilty thief was justified and the guiltless Saviour condemned, that evil-doers might be made righteous through the blood of the Innocent.

Webster 1828 Definition

An evil-doer; a criminal; one guilty of crime and worthy of punishment.

MALEFACTOR, one who does evil; a criminal; an offender against law.

From the Latin male, “ill,” and facere, “to do.”

Two malefactors were crucified with Christ (Luk 23:33).

One railed on Him; the other believed and heard the word of paradise (Luk 23:39).

The accusers called the sinless Christ a malefactor (Joh 18:30).

Key Scripture

Luk 23:32 — "And there were also two other, malefactors, led with him to be put to death."

Luk 23:33 — "And when they were come to the place, which is called Calvary, there they crucified him, and the malefactors, one on the right hand, and the other on the left."

Luk 23:39 — "And one of the malefactors which were hanged railed on him, saying, If thou be Christ, save thyself and us."

Joh 18:30 — "They answered and said unto him, If he were not a malefactor, we would not have delivered him up unto thee."

Modern Corruption

Not a contested doctrine but the plain word for an evil-doer; it recovers the sinless Christ numbered with transgressors and the malefactor saved by grace alone.

expand to see more

The word rebukes a world that calls good evil and evil good. Christ’s accusers stood before Pilate and named the one sinless Man a malefactor — “if he were not a malefactor, we would not have delivered him up” — condemning Righteousness itself and preferring Barabbas the murderer. So the age still arraigns Christ and His holiness as the wrongdoer, and honours the transgressor. To see the Lord of glory numbered with the malefactors and crucified between them is to see the depth of human enmity against God, and the depth of His love, who was made sin for us though He knew no sin.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is grace to the guilty. One malefactor, nailed fast with no hour left to work and no deed to offer, owned his just condemnation, turned to Christ, and prayed to be remembered — and was told, “To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” Here is salvation stripped to its bones: not of works, lest any man should boast, but by a look of faith to the Saviour dying at his side. If a malefactor in his last breath may be received, then no sinner who comes to Christ shall be cast out; but let none presume, for one thief was saved and the other railed and perished.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means an evil-doer, a criminal guilty of crime.

Malefactor — Latin male, “ill,” and facere, “to do.”

It denotes one who does evil, a doer of wickedness.

Two malefactors were crucified with Christ at Calvary (Luk 23:33).

The penitent thief, a malefactor, was received into paradise.

The accusers called the sinless Christ a malefactor (Joh 18:30).

Usage

"Christ was numbered with malefactors, crucified between two, that He might bear their evil."

"A dying malefactor, with no work to offer, was saved by a look to Christ — grace alone."

"The world called the sinless Saviour a malefactor, condemning Righteousness itself."
